summary: Describes a protocol for adding cryptographic signatures and encryption to X.400 content using S/MIME. X.400 is an older messaging system distinct from Internet email, and this lets it use the same security approach.

eli5.summary: An older kind of mail system gets the same locks and signatures as modern email, using this document's instructions.

questions: how to sign x.400 messages with s/mime
which algorithms must x.400 s/mime support
subtitle: How to sign and encrypt the contents of an X.400 message using the same S/MIME and CMS machinery as Internet mail.

tldr.problem: X.400 messaging users wanted signatures and encryption, but the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) offers so many options that independent X.400 systems would not interoperate without a common profile.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC picks a base set of CMS algorithms and attributes, and says to place the ASN.1-encoded X.400 content inside a CMS SignedData or EnvelopedData object, without MIME wrapping unless a 7-bit transport needs it.
tldr.outcome: It gives X.400 and S/MIME agents a shared recipe for secured X.400 content, including the smime-type values signed-x400 and enveloped-x400, and says it adds no new security concerns.

today: RFC 3854 is a Proposed Standard published in July 2004. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. Its companion, RFC 3855, covers how to transport these objects in X.400.

sections.title: Why X.400 Needs an S/MIME Profile
sections.content:
The Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS, RFC 3852) is general enough to protect many kinds of content, and so it offers many options. To make systems in the X.400 community interoperate, RFC 3854 says exactly which CMS features to use when protecting X.400 content. It calls the result CMS-X.400.

The document is meant to be similar to the S/MIME Version 3.1 Message Specification (RFC 3851), except that it is tailored to X.400 content rather than MIME. It applies security to the content of entire X.400 messages, which may or may not be IPMS messages.

It does not address transport. The protected content could travel over Internet mail, X.400 or another suitable transport. Gateway services that relay CMS objects between X.400 and SMTP are explicitly out of scope. A standard MIXER gateway would most likely encapsulate an RFC 822 message carrying CMS objects, which is not a format an X.400 recipient can use.
sections.eli5: Lots of different locks exist, so people who use the old mail system need to agree on which lock and seal to use. This document makes that choice for them.

sections.title: Agents, Compatibility and Terms
sections.content:
The RFC defines a sending agent as software that creates S/MIME CMS objects, a receiving agent as software that interprets and processes them, and an S/MIME agent as user software that is either or both. It follows the rule of being liberal in what you receive and conservative in what you send, so most requirements apply to incoming messages and most recommendations to outgoing ones.

On compatibility, no existing X.400 implementation is believed to support S/MIME version 2, so backward compatibility with version 2 is not a requirement. A goal, if possible, is to stay compatible with existing X.400 implementations that use S/MIME v3.1 wrappers.
sections.eli5: A sender is the person who seals the letter and a receiver is the person who opens it. Be careful when you seal, and forgiving when you open.

sections.title: Required CMS Options
sections.content:
Section 2 sets a base level of algorithm support so all CMS-X.400 implementations can talk to each other.

  • Digest: sending and receiving agents MUST support SHA-1.
  • Signature: receiving agents MUST support id-dsa-with-sha1 (with the parameters absent, not encoded as NULL) and rsaEncryption. Sending agents MUST support either one.
  • Key encryption: both sides MUST support rsaEncryption and SHOULD support Diffie-Hellman.
  • Content encryption: both sides MUST support DES EDE3 CBC (called tripleDES) and SHOULD support AES at key sizes of 128, 192 and 256 bits.

Of the CMS content types, only SignedData and EnvelopedData are used. SignedData applies a digital signature, or in a degenerate case conveys certificates. EnvelopedData provides privacy but, as the RFC notes, does not provide authentication.
sections.eli5: The rules list which kinds of locks and stamps every mailroom must know how to use, so a letter sealed in one place can be opened in another.

sections.title: Signed Attributes
sections.content:
A signature can carry extra signed attributes. Receiving agents MUST be able to handle zero or one instance of each of these, and sending agents SHOULD generate one of each in every CMS-X400 message:

  • signingTime
  • sMIMECapabilities
  • sMIMEEncryptionKeyPreference

Handling of these follows the S/MIME Message Specification. Receiving agents SHOULD also be able to handle zero or one signingCertificate attribute, and sending agents SHOULD generate one. Unknown attributes should be handled gracefully. A sending agent that includes attributes not listed here SHOULD show them to the user so the user knows everything being signed.
sections.eli5: A signed letter can have little notes stuck on it, like the date and which key to answer with. If you add an unusual note, you should show it to the person signing.

sections.title: Building Secured X.400 Messages
sections.content:
An X.400 message has an envelope (handled by the Message Transfer System) and a content (the information the originator wants delivered). This RFC protects the content part. Canonicalization is not required, because X.400 content is a binary rather than a text encoding, and only the embedded content version is used.

Signed-only: SignedData MUST be used. The X.400 content MUST go in the eContent field, keeping the encoding of its content type and not MIME wrapped, and its content type OID MUST go in eContentType. The result is wrapped in a ContentInfo with id-signedData.

Enveloped-only: EnvelopedData is used for confidentiality, with the content placed in encryptedContent. The RFC warns that enveloping without signing gives no integrity, since ciphertext could be replaced so the message is still valid but means something else. A copy of the content-encryption key SHOULD also be encrypted for the originator.

Nesting: layers may be nested. Because version 2 compatibility is of no concern, implementations SHOULD encode the inner object directly as the eContent of the outer one, and MUST be able to process arbitrarily nested structures within reasonable resource limits.
sections.eli5: You can put a letter in an envelope (secret), sign it (proves who wrote it), or both. Just locking a letter does not stop someone from swapping it for a different locked one.

sections.title: Optional MIME Wrapping and Plaintext in SMTP
sections.content:
A signed or enveloped object MAY be wrapped in MIME so that a 7-bit transport can carry it. This outer wrapper sits outside the signature and encryption layers, so gateways can add or remove it along the path. When used, the type is application/pkcs7-mime with smime-type=signed-x400 or smime-type=enveloped-x400 and base64 transfer encoding.

If SMTP carries the result, the optional MIME encoding SHOULD be used. If a binary transport such as X.400 carries it, it SHOULD NOT. In a nested message, the wrapper is only for the outermost layer, and its smime-type follows the innermost protection layer.

For unsecured X.400 content sent over SMTP, the RFC defines Content-Type: application/x400-content with a content-type parameter that is an integer for a built-in type or a dotted OID for an extended type.
sections.eli5: Some mail trucks can only carry plain boxes. So you may put your sealed letter in an outer box for the trip and take the box off at the other end. The seal inside stays untouched.

sections.title: Certificates and X.400 Addresses
sections.content:
S/MIME v3.1 does not say how to get a certificate; it assumes every sending agent already has one. A receiving agent MUST provide some way to retrieve certificates for recipients of encrypted messages. Agents SHOULD let users store and protect certificates of correspondents.

End-entity certificates MAY contain an X.400 address in the form of an ORAddress. It SHOULD be placed in the subjectAltName extension, not in the subject distinguished name, and encoded using the x400Address choice of GeneralName. Receiving agents MUST recognize such addresses.

Sending agents SHOULD make the originator address in the X.400 content match an address in the signer's certificate. Receiving agents SHOULD check that match, and if it fails SHOULD do some explicit alternate processing, such as showing the user the addresses in the certificate.
sections.eli5: A certificate is like an ID card. The mail address on the letter should match the address on the ID card, and if it does not, the reader should be warned.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC says this specification introduces no new security concerns to the CMS or S/MIME models. It points readers to the security sections of the S/MIME Message Specification, the Enhanced Security Services for S/MIME (RFC 2634) and CMS itself.
sections.eli5: Nothing new is risky here. For the usual dangers of locks and seals, read the older rulebooks it points to.

messages.note: Content goes in eContent; eContentType is the X.400 content OID.

messages.label: Step 4: encrypt
messages.note: Encrypted as a single block; contentType is id-signedData.
